results.title: Comparing T-SNE And UMAP: When To Use One Over The Other
results.content:
Title: Comparing T-SNE And UMAP: When To Use One Over The Other
### What Are t-SNE and UMAP? On large datasets, UMAP often runs significantly faster than t-SNE, and in some cases, it can handle millions of points with relative ease. ### Visualizing Data: t-SNE vs UMAP. While t-SNE tends to produce visualizations where clusters seem disconnected or unrelated, UMAP often shows **pathways or transitions** between them, giving a better sense of the overall data landscape. ### Understanding Local Structure: t-SNE or UMAP? If your main goal is to **understand fine local structure**, such as when working with small, tightly-knit clusters, t-SNE’s precise visualizations can offer more insight than UMAP’s broader approach. In some cases, researchers start by using **UMAP** for initial dimensionality reduction due to its **speed** and ability to handle large datasets, and then follow it up with **t-SNE** to fine-tune the local relationships. For instance, you could run UMAP to get a general sense of **clusters** and how they relate globally, and then apply t-SNE to zoom in on **specific sub-clusters** or to further refine the tightness of the local groupings. **What are t-SNE and UMAP used for?**. t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) and UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) are both dimensionality reduction techniques used to visualize high-dimensional data in 2D or 3D. **UMAP** is significantly faster than t-SNE, especially with large datasets. UMAP can handle millions of data points efficiently, whereas t-SNE tends to slow down as the dataset grows. **Does UMAP preserve global structure better than t-SNE?**. **Can t-SNE and UMAP be used together?**. One common approach is to use **UMAP** first for initial dimensionality reduction and then apply **t-SNE** to further refine the visualization of local clusters. **Can I use t-SNE or UMAP for non-visualization purposes?**. Yes, while t-SNE and UMAP are often used for **visualization**, they can also be used for **preprocessing** before clustering or classification tasks by reducing the number of features in a dataset. **Does t-SNE or UMAP work better for imbalanced datasets?**. **UMAP** tends to handle **imbalanced datasets** better than t-SNE because of its ability to maintain global structure while still clustering similar points together. * This article discusses how t-SNE and UMAP are used in **biological data analysis**, particularly in high-dimensional data like single-cell RNA sequencing.

results.title: t-SNE and UMAP | Data Visualization Class Notes
results.content: ## 5.2 t-SNE and UMAP. # 5.2 t-SNE and UMAP. 5.2 t-SNE and UMAP. t-SNE and UMAP are powerful tools for visualizing high-dimensional data in lower dimensions. Understanding how to apply and tune t-SNE and UMAP is crucial for effective data visualization. * t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) and UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) are non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques used for visualizing high-dimensional data in lower-dimensional spaces (typically 2D or 3D). * Both t-SNE and UMAP aim to preserve the local structure of the high-dimensional data in the low-dimensional representation. * t-SNE converts the high-dimensional Euclidean distances between data points into conditional probabilities that represent similarities. * UMAP constructs a weighted k-neighbor graph in the high-dimensional space and then optimizes a low-dimensional graph to be as structurally similar as possible. * Both t-SNE and UMAP have a non-convex optimization objective. ## t-SNE vs UMAP vs PCA. * Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a linear dimensionality reduction technique, while t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear techniques. + t-SNE and UMAP do not rely on linear transformations and can capture more complex, non-linear relationships in the data. * PCA preserves the global structure of the data. * t-SNE and UMAP focus on preserving the local structure. * t-SNE and UMAP are stochastic and can produce different results across runs due to their non-convex optimization. * t-SNE and UMAP are more appropriate for non-linear relationships and complex data distributions. * t-SNE and UMAP are primarily used for visualization purposes. ## Applying t-SNE and UMAP. * The input to t-SNE and UMAP is typically a high-dimensional feature matrix. * Before applying t-SNE or UMAP, it is essential to preprocess the data by scaling the features to a consistent range. * The output of t-SNE and UMAP is a low-dimensional embedding of the data points, usually in 2D or 3D. * t-SNE and UMAP can be applied to various types of high-dimensional data. * Compare the results of t-SNE and UMAP with other dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA). ## Tuning t-SNE and UMAP Hyperparameters. * Consider the computational complexity of t-SNE and UMAP when tuning hyperparameters.

Title: Dimensionality Reduction (UMAP, t-SNE, and PCA) plugin for ImageJ/Fiji - Announcements - Image.sc Forum
# Dimensionality Reduction (UMAP, t-SNE, and PCA) plugin for ImageJ/Fiji. I have just finished a ‘Dimensionality Reduction’ plugin (GitHub repo) for Imagej/Fiji which hopefully some of you will find interesting and useful. The plugin captures data from an open image stack or folder of images and performs one of three dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA, t-SNE, or UMAP) to project the high-dimensional data into a lower dimensional (2D) space that is then plotted onto an ImageJ scatter-plot. ## Using the ‘Dimensionality Reduction’ plugin on an image stack or folder of images. The plugin can be called from a GUI dropdown ‘Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction>…’. ## Using the plugin on non-image data. For convenience, but also because it is an inherently nice way to handle data, to run the plugin on non-image data I recommend encoding that data (e.g. numerical results table/ microarray/ RNA-seq/ or whatever) in an ImageJ image-stack before calling the plugin as usual. Which pulls ONLY NUMERICAL data from an ImageJ results table to build an N stack of nx1 images, where N is the number of samples (stacks) and n is the number of dimensions. **To install the plugin, copy ‘Dimensionality\_Reduction-1.0.0.jar’ to your Fiji plugins folder.**. `Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "PCA no options", dimred.gui.pca_gui. Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "t-SNE with options", dimred.gui.tsne_gui. Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "UMAP with options", dimred.gui.umap_gui. Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "Results to Stack", dimred.gui.results_to_stack. `Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "PCA no options", dimred.gui.pca_gui. Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "t-SNE with options", dimred.gui.tsne_gui. Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "UMAP with options", dimred.gui.umap_gui. Plugins>Dimensionality Reduction, "Results to Stack", dimred.gui.results_to_stack. As a very small update to this thread, i have released a video tutorial for this plugin, showing how to run it on image and non-image data:. This example hopefully also shows how good dimensionality reduction methods, like UMAP, are at identifying structures in the underlying data sets. I have just updated the PCA part of this plugin to allow single or multiple eigenvectors to be output in table or image(stack) form. The new functions of the plugin can be called from the GUI dropdown or via macro script, and here is an example of it running on the traditional Olivetti face stack (400 8-bit faces of 40 people):.
